Game Mastering and Cyberspace

Cyberpunk is an enormously popular genre for roleplaying games. In fact, it’s a primary or secondary influence on science fiction, and even other major genres, in all mediums. It’s part of our fashion and music. It created much of the conceptual framework we use to understand technology. That doesn’t make cyberpunk especially prescient, but the handful of predictions it made have proven alluring as well as practically relevant. We may not want the dystopian parts, but the look, feel, and themes of cyberpunk are apparently irresistible. This chapter is intended to help you navigate it and grab what works for your Modern AGE games. Plus, of course, it includes some new rules.

What is the cyberpunk genre? Where does it come from, and what good is it for roleplaying games? You probably already have some answers for yourself, since we all live in a world influenced by the medium, and new stories and images are easy to come by. That’s why we’re going to concentrate on some of its concrete, historical characteristics, to add to your intuitive impressions. We’ll even add a snappy TL; DR summary for each major point!

Origins

When people talk about where cyberpunk comes from the discussion tends to be wide ranging and greedy at claiming influences and prototypical works. This isn’t wrong—it’s just not especially useful, because after a while we can’t sort superficial resemblances from true progenitors. If we limit ourselves to where the most influential works come from, however, we can make some headway.

In that case, cyberpunk comes from Texas.

Fiction

tl; dr: Describe things like a cyberpunk writer.

To elaborate, we need to back up a bit, to the New Wave movement that shook science fiction in the 60s and 70s. New Wave writers used experimental writing techniques and explored ideas beyond the space opera and science-backed hard SF works that had ruled its literary scene. While this happened around the world, the New Wave hit first and hardest in the UK as Michael Moorcock fostered its development in New Worlds magazine. New Wave influenced authors included John Brunner, who wrote multiple books with proto-cyberpunk themes. One of them, The Shockwave Rider, predicts the invention of worm malware and depicts hacking through the telephone network.

On the other side of the Atlantic, writers influenced by the New Wave developed stylistic and story ideas of their own. The Texas-based Turkey City Writer’s Workshop alumni devised many of the ideas and writing techniques of classic cyberpunk. This group of people included Bruce Sterling and other recognizable names, though not everything sprang from it, and the term “cyberpunk” itself was invented by Bruce Bethke in 1983, for the title of a novel that was never released.

That’s how we get to Texas.

The point of mentioning this goes beyond trivia, however. The Turkey City group associated cyberpunk with a way of writing above and beyond invoking common themes and images. One goal was the “eye kick:” dense, reference-laden, style-soaked prose intended to pack as much atmosphere and information into passages as possible. Look up their writer’s lexicon online, and think about applying its insights to descriptions, plotting, and other aspects of Game Mastering.

Film and Television

tl; dr: Add cyberpunk to another genre to amplify its mood, just like movies do.

While they wouldn’t be recognized as part of a common genre at first, cyberpunk film and television arrived in the 1980s alongside early fiction. This also owes itself to the literary New Wave to a certain extent. Blade Runner was based on Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep by Phillip K. Dick, who was embraced by the New Wave. That film’s director, Ridley Scott, also directed Alien, which made shadowy catwalks, coveralls, and sinister corporations SF film cliches—and of course, Dan O’Bannon wrote the script and did the visual design of the movie after leaving a failed attempt to adapt Dune, a psychedelic New Wave-adjacent novel.

From there, the genre exploded—there are too many influential works to count, especially once the genre made it to the small screen via Max Headroom and other shows. But take a close look at them to see a characteristic of cyberpunk that keeps it vital: Virtually no cyberpunk story is ever just science fiction. The genre is self-consciously postmodern, which means it borrows whatever elements it needs from other genres to enhance its style. Thus, Blade Runner is Noir, as well as cyberpunk. When we say the genre is about style, this is what we mean. Before the New Wave and its descendant, cyberpunk, popular science fiction was generally more concerned with its motifs or the ideas it was trying to present. As GM, you want to go beyond that by emphasizing mood.

Classic Cyberpunk

tl; dr: Look at the earliest versions of cyberpunk cliches and images to help you develop your own takes.

Classic cyberpunk fiction belongs to one of the best-known genres and doesn’t need much explanation. William Gibson invented the term cyberspace, described in a way that would predict or influence the evolution of the Internet and virtual reality, and described the streetwise cyborgs whose descendants can be found all over the place. You can read about the important cyberpunk novels, films, shows, and games of the 80s and 90s anywhere, so there’s not much point reproducing them here. But it is worth noting that as computers became common in households, and hardware development unambiguously obeyed Moore’s Law throughout that era, newer works had to deal with an increasingly technically sophisticated audience, as well as unexpected innovations such as ubiquitous cell phones.

One thing this chapter doesn’t include is game statistics for cyberpunk NPCs and other entities…because we already made that book! Enemies & Allies includes three sections relevant to cyberpunk gaming. The Elite Operatives and The Law and the Lawless present military, police, and criminal figures that only require slight adjustments—maybe a couple of augmentations—for cyberpunk Modern AGE campaigns. The third chapter, Science’s Edge, is explicitly designed to include the near-future characters protagonists might encounter, including high-tech fixers, cyborg hunters, drone-wielding terrorists, and even an augmented fugitive living off the grid. Its various sections appendices include rules for adding extraordinary capabilities to NPCs and other entities of your design. Yes, we’re really pushing this, but that’s because it is extremely useful for cyberpunk-genre games.

Nevertheless, classic cyberpunk follows the esthetics, concerns, and ideas of its times. Images of chrome, monochrome cathode ray tube displays, and soldered circuits appear because they were what cutting edge technology looked like. Cyberspace is either a metaphor for command line shenanigans (in Sterling’s Islands in the Net¸ even fax machines appear prominently) or an alternate realm, largely decoupled from the material world. By 1992, Neal Stephenson’s Snow Crash had consciously harvested (and some say, parodied) these traditions, and at the end of the decade, the final evolution of this era’s cyberpunk cinema appeared in The Matrix.

We often think of older works as potentially problematic, bad at predicting technological developments, and cliché-ridden, but while the first issue is worth tracking, the second doesn’t inherently affect how much you’ll enjoy your game, and the third is only true because those works invented those cliches. Go back to these roots and pay close attention to changes in esthetics. The world is less metallic and monochrome now. Do you want your campaign to look the same, go retro, or mix up new and old?

Multicultural Cyberpunk

Cyberpunk is such an enormous, influential genre that, for brevity’s sake, this section has concentrated on its development in the West, but of course, it’s an international movement.

The biggest influence on cyberpunk from non-English sources is probably manga and anime. Akira, Appleseed, Bubblegum Crisis, and especially Ghost in the Shell present strong visions of the genre, and generally follow the maxim discussed in Classic Cyberpunk by combining cyberpunk concepts with elements from another genre such as Akira’s psychic powers (and in the manga, later development into a full post-apocalyptic setting) and Ghost in the Shell’s procedural stories.

Of course, given the genre’s tendency toward cross-pollination, especially as its ideas have entered the mainstream, it’s hard to tell when a work is primarily cyberpunk, whether it consciously borrows cyberpunk ideas, or whether it just uses similar ideas without any meaningful connection to the genre—and that’s perfectly acceptable. For instance, while the decaying yet transformed Toronto in Nalo Hopkinson’s Brown Girl in the Ring is something cyberpunk fans might recognize, the future in that novel is the backdrop for a story suffused in magical realism.

This kind of mutability not only allows the genre to thrive, but lets people share diverse perspectives through it. We can find stories where crises don’t inevitably lead to cynical exploitation, or where people renew and transform traditions instead of watching them dissolve in the noise of global mass media. Don’t worry though—cyberpunk has room for it all.

Modern Cyberpunk

tl; dr: Everything is cyberpunk now, and that gives you the ability to add anything to your campaign.

Modern cyberpunk usually doesn’t present itself as the sole definite genre of a work, but that’s because so many things are affected by the genre. For instance, the 2011 film The Hunter, based on the 1999 book, takes us alongside the title character stalking an animal in rural Australia. It doesn’t seem very cyberpunk until you learn his mission is to kill the last thyla-cine so a biotech company can patent its venom as a weapon. Cybernetic implants, brain-computer interfaces, powerful corporations—you can find cyberpunk elements spicing up numerous works.

Cyberpunk is increasingly a flavor, not the main course. Powerful corporations, enhanced humans, and artificial intelligence don’t pigeonhole a story as cyberpunk. The central importance of information technology isn’t even fiction. However, even after 40 years (more or less, depending on when you’re reading this and when you think cyberpunk began) an appetite for the full-fledged article remains. We see that in books like Altered Carbon, its sequels, and its television adaptation; in films like Hardcore Henry, Bloodshot (adapted from the Image comic), Upgrade, and of course Blade Runner 2049; and most significantly in games, such as Cyberpunk 2077, a video game based on the longtime R. Talsorian Games roleplaying game, and the Deus Ex series.

Transhumanism

tl; dr: Where early cyberpunk addressed the effects of technology on identity, transhumanism expands this to the destiny of humanity, and what “being human” means.

One of the major influences on later cyberpunk is transhuman ideology: the belief that humans should aggressively use technology to improve ourselves as individuals and a species.

Transhumanism is often associated with the development of strong (truly conscious, but more capable than human) artificial intelligence, and the concept of the technological singularity, where exponentially increasing returns on innovation (exemplified by an artificial intelligence capable of building a superior successor which can also create an AI superior to itself) lead to inconceivably rapid advancement, perhaps to the point of offering us immortality and solving most of our pressing problems.

Transhumanism wasn’t a strong element of early cyberpunk, though even then, there was a sense that access to cosmetic surgery and implants might have a transformational effect on recipients. These early depictions had more in common with ideas of fashion and sexual identity, and while these elements can be part of transhumanism, they don’t inherently accept the movement’s idea that humanity is can be broadly improved beyond changing oneself to adopt the identity best for them. Transhumanism has become prominent enough in science fiction, and even mass culture, that newer works which discuss human augmentation and artificial intelligence are virtually required to grapple with it.

From a Game Master’s perspective, this provides a strong theme for you to address in your games, though it doesn’t mean you have to support transhumanism. What happens when a self-made “subspecies” decides it doesn’t need other humans? When we fuse with artificial intelligence, who’s really going to be in charge? The answers can drive one adventure or an entire campaign.

In classic cyberpunk genre games, information is a world of its own. Data structures appear as objects; applications may look like creatures. The world of information could be a weightless cosmos of abstract geometric designs or appear to be a world like our own—or one with bizarre differences drawn from the minds of programmers, but with equivalent realism. This alternate realm of data, including and transcending the internet we know, is called cyberspace.

Cyberspace is probably the genre’s greatest conceptual contribution to contemporary culture, but much of early cyberpunk was far more concerned with it for the purposes of theme and plotting than how it might work. When William Gibson’s novel Neuromancer came out in 1984, remote use of computers mainly occurred using a mainframe/terminal model, and was mostly restricted to military, government, and academic institutions. An early version of the Internet existed but had no graphical capabilities to speak of. The notion of representing data as images was in its relative infancy; the original Apple Macintosh, the first mass-market personal computer to use a graphical user interface by default, had only been released in January that year.

Subsequent cyberpunk fiction steadily incorporated the evolving presence of personal computers, networks, and their expanding capabilities, so looking back, the genre has given us numerous approaches. Therefore, this chapter provides multiple options for using cyberspace so you can apply whichever ones suit a particular encounter, scenario, or campaign. As GM, you should use whichever is the most convenient in each situation.

For simplicity’s sake, this section assumes time passes in cyberspace at the same subjective pace as it does in the real world. However, this might not be the case, as digital information travels faster than nerve signals—90% of the speed of light compared to about 157-270 miles per hour for brain neurons, slowed even further when we consider the time to translate thought into action through the lower bandwidths of central and peripheral nerves.

You can, instead, decide that subjective time slows in cyberspace. The easiest way is to compare a round in cyberspace to its 15-second counterpart in the physical world. If 1 real round passes for every 15 cyberspace rounds, it means that most cyberspace actions take just one round of “real time,” and a cyberspace round is just one second, one minute in the real world is 15 cyberspace minutes, and so on.

The slower subjective time passes in cyberspace, the more practical it is to have a hacker accompany other characters—but it also means that an entire cyberspace encounter might happen between physical rounds, which is fast in the story, but it slows play at the table, since everyone acting physically must wait for characters in cyberspace to complete several rounds of action.

We don’t recommend you use this kind of time dilation in augmented reality scenarios, where cyberspace exists as an overlay upon the physical world. Furthermore, at the GM’s discretion, some nodes in cyberspace, programs, and other circumstances might slow subjective time compared to reality.

Types of Cyberspace

The varieties of cyberspace present in the genre can be split into three general varieties. These forms of cyberspace aren’t mutually exclusive. In fact, there’s considerable crossover between them, and one system might even be represented by multiple types.

Abstract Cyberspace

Abstract cyberspace is the ultimate evolution of graphical user interfaces, which have exploded into three dimensions, and have the potential to present information for all senses, not just sight and hearing. In abstract cyberspace, a file has a particular shape, color, and position based on the information it contains. A network’s nodes might be large conglomerations of these shapes, connected by paths that describe their connections to other nodes. An experienced hacker memorizes these symbols and can manipulate them faster than using typed or spoken commands.

Bare Cyberspace

Bare cyberspace is just like our own world, where computers don’t present information in the form of perceptible objects by default. Hacking almost always involve typing commands line by line or using various programs. This is the cyberspace of choice for more grounded campaigns, but it is still possible for settings that use it to produce the other forms as an overlay on or subsystem within a computer or network.

Semiotic Cyberspace

Semiotic cyberspace is an alternate reality with objects and entities that might be strange, but still seem at home in some physical realm. One large network might look like a city. Its citizens are data flows and applications. Its security systems look like police officers. Other networks could look like fantasy realms where security privileges are coins guarded by angry dragons, or a gothic castle where users must solve increasingly difficult puzzles to access prized information.

The term “semiotic” refers to the use of symbols, relevant to this form of cyberspace because the true meaning of its digital objects and entities are sometimes difficult to decode. Is a gun a counter-intrusion program, or something used to ban unruly social media commenters?

Manifestations

Cyberspace manifests in one of two ways. Again, there are points where they crossover, and just like in our world, your campaign can feature both.

  • Virtual reality, where the contents of a cyberspace realm are presented as existing in a realm entirely separate from physical existence. Some virtual reality rigs may accept input through physical movement, but it ultimately doesn’t depend on physical space, because it creates a “parallel universe” that’s untethered from our own.
  • Augmented reality, where cyberspace elements are embedded into or overlaid on physical objects and locations. If you want to hack into a building’s maintenance systems and it’s represented by a cyberspace node presented in augmented reality in a closet near its lobby, you must physically enter that location. Whatever technology you’re using to experience cyberspace will display the node there, pegged to its spot by geographical information. Bare cyberspace rarely appears in this fashion, though a terminal window floating in a specific location and viewable with the right equipment is a possibility.

Nature

Lastly, give some thought to the nature of cyberspace. In realistic games, cyberspace is just one way to represent digital information, and outside of bare cyberspace, is mostly intended for end users, who prefer a simple, intuitive way of navigating data. Thus, games, social spaces, and similar spaces might use abstract or bare environments in virtual reality, or overlay them atop real objects in augmented reality, coding and other professional-level data manipulation uses the command line, or, perhaps, simple abstract virtual objects.

In classic cyberpunk, as well as more cinematic or impressionistic portrayals of computing, abstract or semiotic cyberspace represents all information structures by default. Interacting with them not only has effects in the digital realm but changes the data they represent. Burning what looks like a cardboard file folder in cyberspace erases the folder and files they stand for in the system.

Meghan’s starting a cyberpunk campaign and gives some thought to the role of cyberspace. She wants it to be believable, but still include plenty of strange action. She decides that the internet has largely been replaced by the Inter-cosm, a virtual reality of primarily semiotic cyberspace, but with various artistic and professional domains that employ abstract cyberspace. In public domains, cyberspace objects mostly represent themselves, with a few elements that interact with various user settings—shoot a monster, and all you do is affect the representation, as it doesn’t stand for any other data structure. In private realms, however, cyberspace objects might represent critical data, and security programs take various menacing, highly mobile forms.

As mentioned in the beginning of this section, we’re presenting multiple hacking systems so you can employ whichever best fits the current encounter, scenario, or campaign. These systems aren’t mutually exclusive, meaning you can use basic hacking for a quick job, but move into advanced hacking, cyberbreaching, or even virtual combat later in the same session. Before we get into what those mean, however, let’s look at the core traits hacking affects.

The Target: Nodes

A node is a “location” in cyberspace. It can be dedicated hardware, or the data, applications, and various functions of some part of a larger system. It can even be spread out over multiple servers. In game terms, a node is defined by the fact that it requires one successful hack to acquire its privileges. If a system’s security requires you to penetrate multiple layers with separate hacking attempts, each layer is a separate node.

Node Maps

If we think of cyberspace like a classic roleplaying game “dungeon,” nodes are its “rooms,” though their connecting “corridors” have no “width”—you just go to the next connected node with no time in between—and need not obey real-world spatial relationships. When you enter a node without privileges (see Privileges, following) you can access and experience whatever the node permits for users with no special access. If the node permits nothing, it’s a bare address on a screen, a gray, featureless space, or some default virtual environment provided by the node or your own tech.

Like any dungeon, a system in cyberspace has one or more entrances. These indicate nodes that can be directly entered— or invaded—without passing through others in the same system. A public site is a common entry node, as is one only accessible through a terminal inside a secure facility.

Some entry nodes only allow access attempts under certain conditions, such as after receiving biometric data from an authorized user, but the GM should only impose these conditions rarely, since the whole point of hacking is to override these protections. On the other hand, clever characters might fake these requirements, or satisfy them illicitly, using abilities, focuses, and talents unrelated to hacking. This allows non-hackers to contribute. This is the classic scenario seen in William Gibson’s Neuromancer, where the protagonist and their team scheme their way to a terminal in an orbital mansion.

Once you gain the correct privileges in an entry node, you can move to any nodes connected to them. And once you overcome one of those nodes, you open access to the next. It’s just like having to defeat a “monster” or “trap” in one room of the digital dungeon before going to the next.

The Objective: Privileges

A successful hack grants privileges over the compromised node. This typically includes access to the node’s data and functions such as databases, programs, virtual environments, or control over various networked devices, ranging from a humble door to an entire power plant. After gaining control, you might still need specialized knowledge to understand and make use of the node’s privileges. In the power plant example, you might need a special Intelligence focus to understand its controls at all.

Some nodes, such as recreational VR environments, may grant certain privileges to everyone who enters, without requiring a hack. They can stroll on the virtual beach, summon virtual drinks, and go virtual surfing. In these cases, hacking is still required for high level features such as the ability to change the weather, rip personal information from registered users, and so on. There can be various degrees of privilege, but since assigning user privileges is an administrative task, manufacturing or altering them still requires a complete hack of the node.

Of course, the easiest way to get privileges within a node is to earn or steal the proper credentials. If you have the credentials an administrator uses to access a node, you don’t have to hack it, because as far as the node is concerned, you’re supposed to be there. Various forms of social manipulation, theft, and gambits ranging from the prosaic (looking for personal information in the garbage) to bizarre (grafting the cloned face of an administrator onto your own to fool advanced biometric analysis) can acquire these and provide tasks to characters other than dedicated hackers.

IT Traits

As discussed in Chapter 2, information assets, including applications, software, device-running firmware, files, and virtually everything else important enough to get hacked, have specific game traits.

Active Traits

Information resources have the following traits affecting the actions they, or a user operating them, take.

  • Power: Power measures the resource’s brute-force ability to perform its tasks. This modifies the degree of success on a successful roll in every form of hacking except virtual combat, where it modifies damage.
  • Spec: Like Handling for vehicles, this indicates a modifier to tests that use specific, listed focuses with the asset.

Firewall Traits

Information resources sophisticated enough to be involved in hacking have the following defensive traits:

  • Structure: The overall resistance of the data, application, or other information against being altered, copied, deleted, or moved without permission. In virtual combat, Structure is analogous to Health. It also resembles the success threshold in advanced hacking and cyberbreaching, though with a few alterations.
  • Integrity: The data’s ability to fend off incremental or casual intrusion. In virtual combat this is analogous to Toughness, and it also affects other forms of hacking.
  • Crypto: The data’s ability to attain security through cryptographic complexity, determining how hard it is to erode its defenses in the first place. Used as Defense in virtual combat, and as a target number for other forms of hacking.

Basic Hacking

Basic hacking gets its name from its relative simplicity, and the fact that it uses basic tests as described in Chapter 2 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook. Use this system in campaigns where cyberspace is a peripheral element, or in scenarios and encounters where hacking should get a simple answer or benefit. In other words, hacking is useful in these situations, but not central to the story.

To make a basic hacking test, roll Intelligence (Computers) in bare cyberspace, or Accuracy (Virtuality) in semiotic cyberspace + your device or other asset’s test Spec modifier, against a TN equal to your target’s Crypto rating. If you succeed, add your device’s Power rating to the degree of success you scored, but subtract your target’s Integrity. You must both meet or exceed your target’s Crypto and score a modified degree of success of 1 or greater to prevail.

Structure isn’t normally used in basic hacking, but a basic hack against a high Structure target usually takes longer to perform than for a low-Structure target.

Advanced Hacking

Advanced hacking uses advanced tests as described in Chapter 8 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, but with a slight modification: Instead of a normal degree of success threshold, roll 1d6 for each successful roll and add it to the degree of success determined by the Stunt Die, as modified by various factors. Add your device or other IT asset’s Power. Subtract your target’s Integrity. You can also add your focus bonus if you’re level 6 or higher, as detailed on p. 35 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook. Subtract the final total from the Structure of your target. When the hack reduces your target’s Structure to 0, you’ve compromised that system.

Use advanced hacking to represent hacking where time is a factor (such as if you need to disable a room’s security by the time your allies get to its door), but not ones that need to be described in detail.

Cyberbreaching

As you might assume, cyberbreaching uses the breaching test rules in Chapter 8 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook. In this case, use the rules for Advanced Hacking, adding 1d6 and other modifier to your progress, while using the options for required focuses and Tier 1 to 3 consequences from breaching.

Use cyberbreaching when you don’t want to describe a hack in detail, but you want in-the-moment consequences and/or additional specialized knowledge to figure in the attempt.

Virtual Combat

Virtual combat can only take place in abstract or semiotic cyberspace—bare cyberspace doesn’t need this kind of elaboration. In virtual combat opposing security takes the form of combatants who must be defeated to gain privileges.

Movement and Positioning

Movement and relative positions in virtual combat depends on the type of cyberspace used within the node. In addition to the rules below, leaving a node for another, connected node requires a major action, while disconnecting from cyberspace requires two major actions.

Moving in Abstract Cyberspace

Abstract cyberspace is usually laid out on a grid or other symbolic space showing the relationships of virtual objects. Within a node, individuals and objects exist at one of three ranges:

  • Adjacent, indicating they can affect each other with attacks and other actions. It doesn’t matter if the interaction appears to take place across a vast space. If interaction is possible at all, participants are at this range.
  • Within monitoring range, allowing entities to observe, but not affect each other.
  • Out of range completely, where interaction and observation are both impossible.

In most cases, all entities sharing a range with one other entity also share it with each other. Therefore, if you’re attacking the symbolic representation of a file while someone else is repairing it, you are adjacent to the repairer, and can interact with them as well, just as they can interact with you.

A minor action can move you from out of range to monitoring range, or from monitoring range to adjacent range, while a major action can move you from adjacent range to out of range, or vice versa.

An exception to these rules exists in augmented reality, where objects are an overlay on physical reality. In those cases, objects and entities use real-world distances.

Moving in Semiotic Cyberspace

Semiotic cyberspace is real-seeming programmed environment with distances and positions analogous to real space, even if the environment has fantastical elements. You use the rules for movement in Modern AGE, but you gain a Virtual Speed of Perception + 10, except in highly realistic simulations which simulate your real-world Speed.

Attacks and Actions

Attack rolls in cyberspace use Accuracy (Virtuality) and must meet or exceed the target’s Crypto, which acts as their Defense in the virtual realm. This holds true regardless of what the attack looks like, be it with an SMG or poleaxe, unless the GM decides otherwise, such as in a campaign where characters do not realize they’re in a simulation.

Damage

Successful attacks inflict damage equal to the degree of success + 1d6, to the Structure of your opponent’s IT asset, such as one used by an enemy hacker, or one that represents a node’s security. While your degree of success is measured by the Stunt Die, it can be modified by your focus at level 6 and higher, and by your IT asset’s Power, and reduced by your target’s Integrity. Again, this holds true regardless of what the attack appears to be, unless the GM decides otherwise.

The actions listed in Chapter 2 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook can be taken, with the following modifications.

Major Actions

  • All-Out Attack: The Defense adjustment applies to your IT asset’s Crypto.
  • Charge, Run/Chase: Only apply in semiotic cyberspace.
  • First Aid: Unavailable.
  • Defend: Applies to your IT asset’s Crypto.
  • Melee or Ranged Attack: By default, both use Accuracy (Virtuality) and characters can attack any adjacent target in abstract cyberspace, and any target they can perceive in semiotic cyberspace, with the actual appearance being a matter of preference. However, some semiotic simulations may require combatants to equip themselves with virtual counterparts of various weapons with specific ranges. In highly immersive simulations, the GM may allow characters to choose between Accuracy (Virtuality) and

the ability and focus they would use for such a weapon in the real world.

Minor Actions

  • Activate, Aim, Prepare: No changes.
  • Guard Up: Applies to Crypto and attack rolls.
  • Move, Press the Attack: Only apply in semiotic cyberspace. Movement in symbolic cyberspace is covered in Moving in Abstract Cyberspace, previously.
  • Ready: This action is only necessary for nodes with highly realistic semiotic domains, and to switch IT assets, if you have more than one of them at your command. Switching to an IT asset takes one minor action for an asset with a mobile or better interface (see the IT Interface table in Chapter 2), 2 minor actions for an Inconvenient interface, and 1d6+1 minor actions for an Immobile interface. You can swap virtual objects instantly, without using an action, unless a node strongly enforces realistic physics.

Variable Actions

  • Use a Power: Unchanged, though most powers usable in physical space can’t be used in cyberspace.
  • Reload: Only applies in realistic semiotic cyberspace that simulates specific weapons. Otherwise, ignore all prompts to reload.

Hacking Stunts

All forms of hacking, including virtual combat, can utilize the following hacking stunts. The Game Master can allow other stunts from Modern AGE as well, substituting Crypto for Defense, Structure for Health, and Accuracy (Virtuality) for other attack rolls. Social tests typically don’t change in cyberspace, while Perception (Codefinding) usually takes the place of other Perception tests.

Defeat and Recovery

When a target’s Structure drops to 0, anyone capable of interacting with it gains administrative privileges over it, as described in The Objective: Privileges. Be aware, however, that the Exclusive Access hacking stunt allows a target to have 0 Structure in relation to one or more combatants, but not others. Only characters with access to the sum of the damage required to bring the target to 0 enjoy this access.

“Healing” Structure requires administrative access to the target IT asset, be it a node, VR rig, or automated system. Shoring up the systems vulnerabilities requires a TN 11 Intelligence (Computers) test. Success returns Structure equal to your degree of success, as modified by the Power trait of the IT asset they’re using, and other factors. This can be done repeatedly, every 5 minutes (cyberspace subjective time) until you replenish the system’s maximum Structure, which you cannot exceed.

stunt

1+ recompile: You reconstruct your IT asset’s compromised security, recovering Structure equal to the SP you spent. 1-3 active Countermeasures: While hacking, you shore up your own security. Increase your IT asset’s Crypto by the SP you spent against the next attempt to reduce its Structure during the encounter. You may not use this stunt again until after that next attempt. 2Exclusive Access: The damage you did to your target’s Structure, whether through advanced hacking, cyberbreaching, or virtual combat, only applies to your progress toward defeating and gaining privileges over it. As far as other hackers are concerned, the target has not lost the Structure your hacking eliminated. Therefore, if your target’s Structure falls to 0 with the help of your efforts, it is not 0 as far as other hackers are concerned—they must make up the difference themselves. 2Infect: You inflict viruses on your target that slow and disrupt its functions. Reduce its Spec by 2 until the beginning of your next turn. 3Lightning Hack: You work with swiftness and efficiency. You may make another hacking test or virtual combat attack immediately, but you can’t gain or use SP while doing so. 3Recode: You change an element of cyberspace in the node. This can have a purely esthetic effect, or it can interfere with the efforts of another individual in the node as a barrier or distraction that requires them to make a Perception (Codefinding) test versus your Intelligence (Computers) test to take their next action, though neither roll requires an action, and neither one can generate or use SP. 4Damage Power: Your hack corrupts and deletes important utility applications, reducing the target’s Power by 1. While this cannot reduce Power to a negative number, it lasts until the target is overhauled, in a process taking 24 hours of real-world time. 4Damage Integrity: Your hack compromises your target’s security features, reducing its Integrity by 1. This can’t reduce Integrity to a negative number, it lasts until the target is overhauled, in a process taking 24 hours of real-world time. 5Backdoor: Your hack bypasses basic security layers. Ignore your target’s Integrity when inflicting damage against its Structure. 5Exploit: You gain brief access to data or a capability your target has that requires administrative privileges. The Game Master determines the extent of this access, but it ends at the end of your next turn and typically applies to one characteristic, such as the ability to open a door or seize a single file. 6Antipersonnel Countermeasures: You can make an immediate attack against a target’s mind or body, if these are hackable, but you cannot gain or use SP in the attempt. See Hacking the Self for rules.

Hacking the Self

In some campaigns, it’s possible to use cyberspace to kill someone, or hack into their mind through direct neural connections and even particularly sophisticated but non-invasive VR systems. It might even be possible to control someone’s body like a puppet. The Game Master decides which minds and bodies are vulnerable to this form of control, using the following guidelines.

  • Synthetic bodies with the Hackable vulnerability (see ABIOTIC VULNERABILITIES in Chapter 1) can be hacked. This doesn’t confer the ability to hack into minds. In some campaigns it might be possible to hack into anyone’s body if the hacker can gain access.
  • The hacker requires access. This may require specialized “brainwashing” equipment, the very IT device the target uses to access cyberspace, or an augmentation capable of transmitting and receiving digital information. At the GM’s discretion, some, or all, of following augmentations in Chapter 2 might have this vulnerability: AV Memory, Bionic Ear, Bionic Eye, Brain Backup, Commlink, Computer Processor, Focus Program, Kill Switch, and Memory Implant.

Game Systems

The largest impediment to hacking a target’s mind or body is the information tech they use to interact with cyberspace. If the route to the target’s mind or body is provided or mediated by an IT asset as described in Chapter 2 and the rules here, the hacker must reduce its Structure to 0 before reaching through to the operating character. If there isn’t an IT asset, or if it’s a simple device without special traits such as Structure, no impediment exists. Thus, while hackers might be vulnerable to attack through their rigs, they also provide a measure of protection. Assets which don’t require an intimate neural or sensory connection do not provide a path to compromise the user. The GM determines when this is a factor on a case-bycase basis. But once the hacker drops the intervening device’s Structure to 0, they gain direct access to the target character until the end of the encounter, even if the device’s Structure is restored during this time.

If these conditions are met, a hacker can use advanced hacking or virtual combat, as decided by the GM. Basic hacking should only be permitted for minor NPCs, and cyberbreaching

In campaigns that use semiotic cyberspace, hacking the mind might involve entering a “node” projected by the target’s mind, containing their memories, desires, and imaginings—and possibly, dangerous representations of the target’s desire to defend themselves. As noted in Game Systems, cyberbreaching is only used to hack minds in exceptional circumstances—but in those circumstances, weaponized thoughts might appear as consequences for failed tests. These hardened minds may also generate additional combatants in the mental realm.

should be reserved for targets with special characteristics, such as a target with special implanted or psychologically conditioned countermeasures.

Hacking rolls must meet or exceed a TN of the target’s Intelligence + 10, representing the ability to detect intruding thoughts and impulses, imagine countermeasures, and visualize ways to deceive the intruder. This replaces the Crypto trait. Reduce a successful roll’s degree of success by the target’s Willpower, which replaces IT device Integrity.

Leftover degrees of success and virtual combat damage can be used for the following purposes:

  • Injury: The hack manipulates voluntary and autonomic functions to injure the target by causing abnormal cardiac activity, strokes, muscle contractions strong enough to produce self-injury, and even instances of self-harm. Degrees of success become penetrating wound damage.
  • Subversion: The hack has no cumulative effect, but when it accumulates degrees of success equal to the target’s Health, they become compromised, as per Outcomes, following.

Outcomes

Inflicting injury doesn’t allow progressive control of the target—once their Health drops to 0, they lose consciousness and begin dying according to the rules of Modern AGE.

Subverting the target to the point where they become compromised, however, grants “administrative access” to the target’s mind and body. Because this requires as much effort as it would take to simply kill the target, its capabilities are potent. The hacker might operate the target’s body by remote control, implant a completely new identity, subtly alter memories, and so on. The exact extent of control is left to the GM, but they should strongly consider players’ willingness to lose control of their characters, and the actions they would find acceptable as players (regardless of what their characters would think) in the game. Do not allow, or enact, anything that would genuinely upset them, as opposed to feeling a sense of dramatic tragedy, or disappointment that their characters failed to escape this fate. Merciful GMs may allow tests to resist at regular time intervals or give the control a finite duration.

The type of connection that enabled the hack determines what it can do. A character with an organic mind but a hackable synthetic body might be operated like a puppet, but the hacker has no access to their mind. Expertise and resources are also considerations. Hacking a mind isn’t like hypnosis, where a semi-voluntary subject fills in the blanks in simple verbal commands. Commands, memory implants, and so on, must be specific and complete. Memories need to be built the way a digital VFX artist alters and creates images. Complex somatic commands, such as engaging in combat, may require the target to be “piloted” remotely. Automation (see Chapter 2) can greatly simplify these tasks.

Finally, hackers are limited by the target’s overall experience and competence. This is purely a game consideration that prevents characters from using mind hacking to give themselves extra talents, focuses, and so on. It may, however, be possible to swap game traits around instead.
